meta.title: Proving the Frontline Loop in Weeks
meta.subtitle: A narrow pilot for 120 APAC stores and 2,000 frontline staff

slides.title: Proving the Frontline Loop in Weeks
slides.subtitle: A narrow pilot for 120 APAC stores and 2,000 frontline staff
slides.script: We are here to make this practical for RetailCo. We are not proposing a long platform programme that only becomes useful next year. We are proposing a tight first phase in a handful of stores, built around the four pains we heard from the COO: floor visibility, the 3x gap between managers, six-week onboarding, and painful roster coordination. The point is to prove a working loop quickly: see what happens, hear what is said, capture what works, and turn that proof into the rollout proposal.

slides.text: We can prove the frontline loop in weeks, not wait for a platform programme next year.
slides.script: We believe the fastest route to confidence is a deliberately narrow pilot. RetailCo already has 120 stores and 2,000 frontline staff, so a big-bang transformation would create complexity before it creates learning. Instead, we start where the operating questions are clearest. We pick a small store set, instrument the moments that matter, compare what strong teams do differently, and package the evidence. That gives us a decision point in weeks: expand, adjust, or stop based on RetailCo’s own frontline proof.

slides.quote: I have no idea what actually happens on my shop floor. I get a spreadsheet on Monday about last week.
slides.script: This is the first problem because it sets the clock speed for every other decision. If we only understand last week on Monday, we are always managing after the fact. We can see missed service moments, queue pressure, conversion behaviours, and staff activity only once the chance to correct them has passed. Spacesight changes that timing. It gives RetailCo a way to see what is happening on the floor while it still matters, so store conversations can move from opinion to observed reality.

slides.text: The cost of lag is decisions made after the customer has already left.
slides.script: When the signal arrives late, the cost is not only reporting frustration. It is the lost ability to coach in the moment, test a change during the trading week, or spot a pattern before it becomes normal. A Monday spreadsheet may explain what happened, but it cannot help a store manager recover the Saturday peak. That is why the pilot should not begin with dashboards for headquarters. It should begin with a practical loop in stores where the data can change behaviour the same day.

slides.label: Floor events visible while they still matter
slides.script: Spacesight is the first fix in the loop because it gives RetailCo eyes on the shop floor. We use in-store vision analytics to surface what is actually happening during trading, not as a retrospective spreadsheet. The value mechanism is simple: if a pattern is visible today, the store leader can respond today. We would use the pilot to identify which floor signals matter most for RetailCo, how they are reviewed, and what action store teams can realistically take without adding another layer of admin.

slides.text: The 3x gap is not a talent mystery; it is an operating system waiting to be captured.
slides.script: The second problem is the difference between the best and worst store managers. RetailCo described that gap as 3x, which is too large to treat as personality alone. Somewhere inside the best stores are routines, language, coaching habits, and customer interactions that others could copy if we could capture them clearly. Echo and Harbor Wiki work together here. Echo helps us hear and score the customer conversation. Harbor Wiki turns the best observed behaviours into a living playbook that managers and staff can actually use.

slides.title: Every COO pain has a named answer

rows.right: Spacesight shows what happens in-store during trading.
Echo and Harbor Wiki capture repeatable selling behaviours.
Harbor Wiki gives new hires one trusted operating playbook.
Open item: scheduling workflow, no roster product in scope.
Alivia packages pilot evidence into the client proposal.

slides.script: We are being explicit about the mapping because this is where pilots either stay useful or become theatre. Spacesight answers the visibility gap. Echo and Harbor Wiki answer the 3x manager gap by capturing what strong performance sounds like and how it is done. Harbor Wiki also reduces dependence in onboarding by giving new hires a trusted place to learn the RetailCo way. Scheduling is different. We do not have a roster engine in this product set, so we would treat roster coordination as an open workflow item and connect pilot findings to that decision separately.

slides.text: New hires should learn from RetailCo’s best day, not whoever happens to be rostered.
slides.script: The onboarding pain is especially important because RetailCo has 2,000 frontline staff across APAC. When a new hire takes six weeks to become productive and the experience depends on whoever is working that day, the business is relying on chance. Harbor Wiki gives us a place to bottle the routines from the best managers, the strongest customer conversations, and the store practices that Spacesight and Echo reveal. We are not replacing local coaching; we are giving local coaches one consistent source of truth to work from.

slides.title: Pilot proof target
slides.label: stores in the first phase
slides.note: A small sample is enough to prove the loop before broader rollout.
slides.script: We would recommend five stores for the first phase because the goal is proof, not coverage. Five is enough to include different store contexts, compare stronger and weaker operating patterns, and keep the work close enough that we can learn quickly. The proof we want is not a generic ROI model. It is RetailCo evidence: what Spacesight surfaced, what Echo heard, what Harbor Wiki captured, and whether managers and new hires could use that knowledge during the week rather than waiting for Monday’s spreadsheet.

slides.title: The loop we prove before scaling

steps.label: Observe
steps.text: Spacesight shows floor reality during trading.

steps.label: Bottle
steps.text: Harbor Wiki turns best actions into guidance.

steps.label: Package
steps.text: Alivia converts evidence into a proposal.

slides.script: This is the operating loop we want the pilot to prove. First, we observe the floor with Spacesight so we know what is actually happening. Then we hear the customer interaction through Echo, because the difference between good and great often lives in the conversation. Next, we bottle the best repeatable behaviours in Harbor Wiki, so staff and managers have something concrete to use. Finally, Alivia turns the evidence into a proposal for the next phase, including what we learned about the adjacent scheduling workflow.

slides.title: Approve Phase 1, then decide at checkpoint
slides.subtitle: A narrow start, a clear proof point, and no commitment to a year-long programme upfront
bullets: Select five APAC stores for pilot
Run Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki together
Review proof and scheduling open item
Use Alivia for the rollout proposal
slides.script: Our ask is to approve Phase 1 as a focused pilot, not a full rollout. We jointly select five APAC stores, run Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki as one loop, and agree the evidence we need before we start. At the checkpoint, we review what became visible, what top managers do differently, whether the onboarding playbook is usable, and how the roster coordination issue should be handled. If the proof is strong, Alivia packages the rollout proposal so RetailCo can scale with confidence.

approach.angle: Argue speed to value: a narrow pilot in a handful of stores that proves the loop in weeks, not a platform programme that lands next year.
approach.device: Problem, then what it actually costs, then what fixes it, then proof. Repeat tightly.
approach.opener: Open with the one sentence you want them to remember, then justify it.
approach.close: Close on a phased rollout with a clear first phase and a checkpoint.
